newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mrs Clinton to see shrines to apartheid struggle.
newsitem.headline: Mrs Clinton to see shrines to apartheid struggle.

text.p: U.S. First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton was due to arrive in South Africa on Tuesday for a tour which will include visits to shrines to the struggle against white oppression.

Mrs Clinton, on the first tour of Africa by a sitting U.S. first lady, was scheduled to lay a wreath to commemorate the deaths of hundreds of people killed by apartheid police during an uprising in Soweto township two decades ago.
She was also expected to meet President Nelson Mandela in Cape Town and visit the island jail which was his home for 18 of the 27 years he spent behind bars for fighting apartheid.

Mrs Clinton, accompanied by her 17-year-old daughter Chelsea, was to visit Soweto, the sprawling black city near Johannesburg where nearly 700 people died in several weeks of protest against white domination in 1976 -- most of them shot by police.

The demonstrations began with a march by pupils against a government decision to force the use of the Afrikaans language in schools. Police opened fire on the marchers and Hector Petersen, 13, was the first to die.
His grave is a major monument to those who died in the fight against white domination and Mrs Clinton was to lay a wreath at the spot, as well as visit a school and a children's home.

On Wednesday the first lady heads for Cape Town, where she will meet Nobel peace laureate Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who now heads South Africa's "truth commission" into human rights abuses during 30 years of fighting over apartheid racial segregation.
She will meet Mandela on Thursday, when she will also visit Robben Island -- South Africa's Alcatraz.
Many black activists, including Mandela and other members of the post-apartheid government in Pretoria, languished there under white rule.
Mrs Clinton's African tour is her ninth solo trip outside the United States. The two-week goodwill mission began on Monday in Senegal and includes Zimbabwe, Uganda, Tanzania and Eritrea.
In Senegal she visited a slave house that was the exit point for Africans bound for a life of slavery in North and South America and the Caribbean.

Mrs Clinton, who delayed the start of her trip by one day to tend to President Bill Clinton as he recovers from knee surgery, said her husband had told her not to cancel her trip because of his injury.
